general.temas: Recurring stories include the court-appointed administration of Revolut amid a money-laundering investigation, the investigation into former police chief De Gennaro over the alleged misdirection of inquiries into the Via D’Amelio massacre, and the debate over taxes on great fortunes. Bomb threats against schools and the migration agreement with Rwanda also feature. Only Corriere della Sera highlights the Liguria case and Toti’s meetings with businessman Spinelli.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions are considerable because of the investigations involving Liguria, Revolut and the alleged misdirection of inquiries into the Via D’Amelio massacre. In politics, the clash between governing coalition partners over the Superbonus and the drinks tax stands out, as do differences between opposition parties over wealth taxes. Threats against schools and some polarizing headlines add to public anxiety. News about sport, savings and pay rises for healthcare workers partly offsets that climate.

Corriere della Sera.resumen:
- Changes to the highway code and doubts about their effect on victims.
- Meetings on a yacht and alleged manipulation of COVID data in Liguria; the mayor of Genoa calls for clarity and denies having favored Spinelli.
- Tensions within the governing majority over the Superbonus and the drinks tax; a column criticizes the accumulation of debt.
- Russia advances toward Kharkiv and Zelensky acknowledges that the situation is very difficult.
- Fedez denies being involved in the Iovino case; the tax authorities demand money from Camila Giorgi. Investment advice is also offered.
Corriere della Sera.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “attacks,” “the case erupts” and “pursued by the tax authorities” dramatize some issues, although there is no discernible appeal to the people against the elites.
Corriere della Sera.sesgo: The front page highlights possible irregularities in Liguria and conflicts within the governing majority, taking a critical approach to public administration. It also includes accounts and statements from those involved.

la Repubblica.resumen:
- Revolut faces court-appointed administration and a money-laundering investigation; the front page examines its business model.
- Conte proposes a tax on the super-rich and another article analyzes Schlein’s strategy.
- Former police chief De Gennaro is under investigation for an alleged cover-up in the Via D’Amelio massacre case.
- A third bomb alert affects schools; the account of a rabbi who was assaulted is also included.
- The front page addresses Britain’s rapprochement with the EU and the debate over the right to be forgotten and newspaper archives.
la Repubblica.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “memory under attack,” “a weapon against newspapers and archives” and “Report sinks” use alarmist or sensationalist language.
la Repubblica.sesgo: The front page gives space to center-left politics and takes a critical approach to the use of the right to be forgotten in ways that could affect newspaper archives. Coverage of Revolut combines its achievements with its legal troubles.

La Stampa.resumen:
- Healthcare: pay rises are announced for doctors and nurses; disagreements with the regions over their funding and the bonus for older people are also reported.
- Revolut is placed under court-appointed administration in an alleged money-laundering case involving an aggravating mafia connection; its services will continue to operate, according to the company.
- De Gennaro is under investigation for an alleged cover-up in the Via D’Amelio massacre case. New bomb threats affect hundreds of schools.
- The front page addresses inequalities in personal income tax and the debate over a tax on the super-rich and opposition unity.
- The University of Turin condemns a professor’s remarks about an accident involving graffiti artists; in sport, Cobolli faces Medvedev.
La Stampa.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “paradoxes and injustices” and the quotation of the threats introduce emotional and alarming emphasis.
La Stampa.sesgo: The selection pays particular attention to healthcare, taxes and the consequences of the Revolut case for customers. A critical approach to tax inequalities and the opposition’s difficulties is discernible, but this does not establish an overall political orientation.

Il Giornale.resumen:
- A farewell to Toni Capuozzo and an investigation into the Via D’Amelio massacre and Borsellino’s red diary.
- Headlines critical of Islam and a warning about the alliance between religion and Marxism in Iran.
- Revolut placed under administration for a year, and news about the mafia, businesses and tax evasion.
- Possible meeting between Putin and Xi, with Ukraine and Europe’s role in the foreground.
- The EU is considering migrant centers in Rwanda, following the Italian model in Albania.
Il Giornale.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “the weapons of Allah that Italy does not want to see” and “the new Yalta that disarms Europe and corners it” use alarmist and confrontational language, although other headlines are informative.
Il Giornale.sesgo: The front page takes a critical approach to Islam and to what it presents as Italy’s failure to pay attention to its risks. In international politics, it emphasizes a view of Europe as harmed by the decisions of the great powers.

Il Fatto Quotidiano.resumen:
- Five European countries are preparing an agreement with Rwanda to send migrants they want to expel there; the European Commission backs it.
- The opposition debates taxes on great fortunes, while an article warns of the electoral risks of its healthcare approach.
- An anti-mafia operation in Bari results in 19 arrests; in Angri, authorities are investigating the fatal stabbing of a woman.
- The RAF quadrupled its reconnaissance missions over Kaliningrad in October.
- Alcaraz beats Tiafoe at the ATP Finals; controversies on the program “Ballando con le Stelle” also feature prominently.
Il Fatto Quotidiano.motivo_populismo: Informative headlines predominate, although expressions such as “overwhelms,” “exasperated neighbors” and the detail of a student being “impaled” add drama and sensationalism, without an explicit confrontation between the people and the elites.
Il Fatto Quotidiano.sesgo: The selection combines politics and international affairs with crime stories and television controversies, often in an eye-catching style. Opinion pieces on healthcare and television take explicit positions, but no unequivocal overall political orientation is apparent.

opiniones.comunista:
I see a class question in the debate over healthcare and taxes: who produces the wealth, and who decides how it is used? As pay improvements for doctors and nurses and the future of subsidies for specialist appointments are debated, taxing large financial fortunes should not be taboo. Healthcare and the conditions of those who provide it are collective needs, not budget items to be pitted against one another.

I support that tax, but I am not satisfied with redistributing a small portion of wealth after capital has decided its fate. I advocate adequately funded public services and collective ownership, under democratic control, in essential sectors. Revolut’s court-appointed administration is also a reminder that financial innovation is no substitute for public oversight. The working class needs rights and decision-making power, not just promises of prosperity.
opiniones.anarquista:
I read that several parties are debating taxes on great fortunes. Reducing inequality matters, but I do not trust that delegating every decision to the state and waiting for the next electoral pact will be enough to end the power that wealth concentrates. I prefer a society where those who work and sustain our shared life directly control their resources, through free associations and shared decisions.

I also read that several European countries are preparing an agreement with Rwanda to send migrants they want to expel there. It strikes me as a way of removing from our sight people whose freedom should matter as much as our own. In the face of borders managed from above, I advocate networks of welcome and mutual aid built by those who live in these communities and those who arrive in them. Collective freedom cannot be built on exclusion.
opiniones.liberal:
The proposal to tax large financial fortunes is presented as a fair solution, but I see a risk: punishing saving and investment without addressing the underlying problem, which is how much the state spends and with what results. I prefer low, simple and predictable taxes that give people more freedom to decide what to do with their money.

The debt debate points in the same direction. Spending today without explaining who will pay tomorrow is not solidarity, but a transfer of responsibility. A limited state should properly fund its essential functions, be accountable and avoid privileges. I also trust competition to improve financial services, provided companies obey the law and answer for their actions. Economic freedom requires clear rules and personal responsibility, not favors or impunity.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I believe Italy must regain control of its borders. The agreement five European countries are preparing with Rwanda points in the right direction: anyone who has no right to stay must be returned, with clear procedures and legal safeguards. But our migration policy cannot depend on Brussels finally realizing the need to act. A state that does not decide who enters and who stays relinquishes an essential part of its sovereignty.

I also demand a state that is tough on crime and transparent with its citizens. The investigation into possible misdirection in the Via D’Amelio massacre case must be pursued to the end, while respecting the presumption of innocence. Authority is not defended by concealing responsibility: it is strengthened when it shows that the law also reaches those in the highest offices.
opiniones.centro:
I worry that the debate over wealth is being reduced to a choice between punishing success and tolerating inequality. The proposal to tax large financial fortunes deserves to be studied without prejudice, but also rigorously: it matters how the tax would be collected, what effects it would have on investment and which services the revenue would fund. I prefer a stable and understandable tax agreement to a grandiose promise.

I also believe the Revolut case is a reminder of why innovation needs oversight. The court-appointed administration must run its course without turning an investigation into a premature conviction; at the same time, customers deserve clear information and effective controls. An open market works better when there are reliable rules and authorities capable of enforcing them. Defending institutions does not mean giving them a blank check, but demanding transparency and accountability from them.
